titre: Fourth Floor, Pronounced Three Different Ways
accroche: In New York, in 1962, the same question put to salespeople in three department stores does not get quite the same answer.
contenu_vulgarise:
In November 1962, a man walks into three department stores in Manhattan and asks dozens of saleswomen the same question: “Excuse me, where are the women's shoes?” The answer is almost always the same: “Fourth floor.” He pretends not to have heard; they repeat it, more carefully this time. He is neither a lost customer nor a satisfaction surveyor. He is linguist William Labov, who has just found a way to measure, without anyone noticing, one of the most sensitive social markers of New York English: the presence or absence of the r after a vowel, as in fourth or floor.

## Three Stores, One Gesture

Labov chooses his three sites with care: Saks Fifth Avenue, the most expensive and prestigious store in his sample; Macy's, at Herald Square, a mid-range store; S. Klein, on Union Square, a low-priced store frequented by working-class customers. The protocol is identical everywhere: the same question, asked on the same floor, of employees who do not know they are taking part in a study. In all, 264 people answer (68 at Saks, 125 at Macy's, 71 at Klein) for a little over six hours of recording.

The result is clear. The r after a vowel, pronounced at least once in the four opportunities offered by “fourth floor” said twice, appears among 62% of Saks employees, 51% of Macy's employees, and only 20% of Klein employees. The ranking follows exactly the social ranking of the three stores. And that is not all: in all three stores, the second answer, pronounced with more care, contains more r's than the first. Proof that speakers know, without ever having been taught, which pronunciation is perceived as the most careful.

## What This Shifts

The received idea is that an accent is a matter of the person, of region of origin, of biographical chance. Labov's study shows something else: the same person, in the same place, modulates their pronunciation according to context, and this modulation follows a social hierarchy that everyone recognizes without ever having consciously learned it. The r is not distributed at random: it works as a sign of prestige, almost as precisely as a price in a shop window. And it is this result, obtained without interviewing anyone, without a questionnaire, without any subject knowing they were speaking for science, that underpins much of modern sociolinguistics: the idea that a variation in pronunciation, however slight, can be studied with the same rigor as a social fact.

repere.texte: In November 1962, William Labov questions 264 salesmen and saleswomen in three department stores in Manhattan on the sole basis of an innocuous question: “where are the women's shoes?” The r pronounced after a vowel, as in fourth floor, appears among 62% of employees at Saks (the most expensive store), 51% of those at Macy's, and 20% of those at S. Klein (the least expensive): in the exact order of the three stores' social ranking.
repere.source: William Labov, The Social Stratification of (r) in New York City Department Stores, 1966

carte.punch: A saleswoman pronounces the r of fourth floor more often at Saks than at Kleins, without knowing it.
carte.idee: In 1962, William Labov questions 264 saleswomen in three New York department stores with a single innocuous question. The r pronounced after a vowel appears among 62% of employees at the most expensive store, 51% at the mid-range store, 20% at the cheapest: in the order of the stores' prestige.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The rest of Labov's career, from New York to Philadelphia, and the studies that extended this method.

quiz.question: What does Labov's study in the three New York department stores show, in 1962?
choix: That all New Yorkers pronounce the r the same way, whatever their store or social position
That the pronunciation of the r depends solely on the speaker's geographic origin, regardless of context
That the saleswomen questioned were aware of taking part in a linguistic study, which skewed their answers
That the same pronunciation trait varies with the store's prestige and the care taken in the answer, without speakers being aware of it
quiz.explication: The r of fourth floor is pronounced by 62% of Saks employees (the most prestigious store), 51% of Macy's employees, and only 20% of S. Klein employees (the cheapest), and even more when the question is asked again with more care. It is therefore neither a uniform usage nor a mere marker of geographic origin independent of context. And Labov's method consists precisely in questioning employees without their knowing they are part of a study: this is what guarantees spontaneous answers, unbiased by observation.
